summary: A man arrested after a facial-recognition misidentification sued the police for false arrest; the case is pending, with civil-liberties groups filing in support.

An energy company won a large defamation verdict against an environmental organisation, a suit widely described as meant to silence it; the award was reduced and is on appeal, and the organisation has countersued.
Church of Scientology officials were convicted for infiltrating and burglarising federal agencies to remove records critical of the church, and for organised harassment of critics.
Denmark's data-protection authority suspended a municipality's use of Google Workspace in schools until it assessed the risks of transferring pupils' data properly.

The UK Information Commissioner fined Clearview AI £7.5 million for processing UK residents' faces without a lawful basis; a tribunal later set the fine aside, and the regulator's appeal succeeded in 2025.
WhatsApp sued the maker of Pegasus spyware for breaking into about 1,400 phones, including journalists' and activists'; a jury found it liable, the damages were cut, and the case is on appeal.
A man wrongly arrested after a facial-recognition match sued the city of Detroit; the case settled in 2024 with a payment and new limits on police use of the technology.

Challengers asked France's highest administrative court to stop Microsoft Azure hosting the national health-data platform after the EU's top court struck down US data transfers; the court refused but ordered extra safeguards.
Italy's data-protection authority fined Clearview AI €20 million and ordered it to stop processing and delete Italians' facial data.
The EU's highest court struck down the EU–US Privacy Shield for sending Europeans' data to the US, while upholding standard contract clauses with conditions.
France's data-protection authority fined Clearview AI €20 million for collecting faces without a legal basis and ordered it to stop and delete them.
The EU's highest court struck down the Safe Harbour arrangement for sending Europeans' data to the US.

An oil company won a racketeering judgment against a lawyer who had litigated against it, and he was later convicted of criminal contempt; his supporters describe the prosecution as retaliation, while the courts' findings went against him.

eBay employees ran a campaign of harassment and covert surveillance against journalists who covered the company; seven pleaded guilty, eBay paid a $3 million criminal fine, and the civil case settled.
Context, not a case: the East German Stasi's documented method of covertly breaking down targets' lives, recorded in German state archives.
Clearview AI appealed the UK fine and won before a tribunal, which held that UK law did not reach its work for foreign governments; that ruling was later overturned.
Australia's Information Commissioner found Clearview AI collected Australians' faces without consent and ordered it to stop and destroy them.
The State of Vermont sued Clearview AI under consumer-protection and data-broker law; the case is recorded as pending, its current status not yet verified.
Chicago residents challenged police stops prompted by ShotSpotter gunshot alerts; the settlement holds that an alert alone does not justify a stop or frisk.
A man charged with murder on the strength of a ShotSpotter alert, later dropped, sued Chicago; the city made a $500,000 offer of judgment.
Campaigners sought the release of the UK's COVID-19 data contracts with technology firms including Palantir; the contracts were published and the government agreed to consult before extending them.
The UK Information Commissioner appealed and the Upper Tribunal held that UK data-protection law does apply to Clearview AI, sending the fine back to be decided again.
Residents challenged Norfolk, Virginia's network of Flock licence-plate cameras as an unconstitutional search; the court upheld it and the residents are appealing.
A man jailed after a Clearview AI facial-recognition match sued the sheriff's office for false arrest and malicious prosecution; the case settled in 2025.
France's data-protection authority imposed a further €5.2 million penalty because Clearview AI had not complied with its 2022 order.
The Dutch data-protection authority fined Clearview AI €30.5 million for its facial database and warned of further penalties for non-compliance.
Chile's Supreme Court ordered a neurotechnology company to delete a user's brain data, granting a constitutional protection claim.
Campaigners began a legal challenge to the NHS's £330 million data-platform contract with Palantir, questioning its legal basis and consultation; there is no judgment yet.
The US Federal Trade Commission found Rite Aid's in-store use of facial recognition unfair, including biased errors, and banned it from using the technology for five years.
A privacy group sued Immigration and Customs Enforcement for records about Palantir's FALCON system; the case settled with documents released.
A nationwide class sued Clearview AI under Illinois's biometric-privacy law; the settlement gives the class a share of the company's value, approved in 2025.
A woman arrested after a facial-recognition misidentification sued Detroit for false arrest; the case was dismissed in 2025 and she is appealing.
Hewlett-Packard investigators obtained board members' and journalists' phone records by deception; HP paid $14.5 million to settle California's case.

Plaintiffs sued Clearview AI in California, saying its face collection violates the state constitution, unfair-competition law and civil rights; the case is recorded as pending, docket not yet verified.
A challenger asked the EU General Court to annul the EU–US Data Privacy Framework; the court dismissed the action in 2025 and an appeal is expected.
Greece's data-protection authority fined Clearview AI €20 million and ordered it to stop processing and delete Greeks' facial data.
A US political party sued over FBI surveillance and disruption, including burglaries, informants and mail-opening; the court held the FBI liable and awarded damages.
Germany's data-protection authorities concluded that Microsoft 365 could not be shown to be run in compliance with EU data-protection law; no fine was involved.
Oracle protested the Pentagon's JEDI cloud contract process; the protest was denied and the denial upheld on appeal.
The EU's data-protection supervisor found the European Commission's use of Microsoft 365 broke EU data rules and ordered corrections, which the Commission met in 2025.
Amazon Web Services challenged the award of the Pentagon's JEDI cloud contract to Microsoft, alleging improper influence; the case ended when the contract was cancelled in 2021.
Canada's privacy commissioners found Clearview AI collected Canadians' faces without consent and recommended it stop and delete them.

Undercover police officers infiltrated UK activist groups for decades, some deceiving women into relationships; the police apologised and settled, a tribunal found serious rights breaches, and a public inquiry continues.
Civil-liberties groups sued Clearview AI under Illinois's biometric-privacy law; the 2022 settlement bars it from selling its face database to most private companies in the US.
A Swiss court found that Nestlé and a security firm unlawfully infiltrated an activist group writing a critical book, and ordered damages.
An immigrant-rights legal group sued for records about Palantir systems used by Immigration and Customs Enforcement; the case was filed in 2026 and is pending.
